iv). That many of the material and charge-sheet witnesses have been withheld without any explanation by the prosecution and as such non-production of such witnesses should have given rise to an adverse presumption against the prosecution case and the accused appellants ought to have been given benefit of doubt. 

 24. Now, the last submission on behalf of the appellants is that the prosecution has failed to produce some material and charge-sheet witnesses in this case and for their non-production an adverse presumption ought to have been drawn against the prosecution case. It is true that out of 23 charge sheet witnesses only 13 witnesses have been produced. It is well-settled in view of section 134 of the Evidence Act that the prosecution is not bound to produce all the witnesses in the charge sheet and it is the quality of the evidence and not the quantity that has to be taken into consideration in weighing the evidence of the prosecution. Even on the basis of the evidence of a single witness if wholly reliable the conviction of the accused can be maintained. On our scrutiny of the order-sheet of the case we find that for some reasons the prosecution filed an application before the Sessions Judge for exemption of appearance of some of the charge sheet witnesses. Firstly, the prayer was refused by an order dated 27.6.85 but again there was another application by the prosecution alleging that about 7 witnesses namely Jamila Khatun, Nowsher Ali, Abdul Quddus, Nalu Mia, Abdur Rashid, Abdul Malek and Alam Miawere gained over by the defence and as such the prosecution sought exemption of their production in Court and the prayer was allowed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge by his order dated 16.7.85. Thus it appears there are sufficient reasons for non-producing the said charge-sheet witnesses in this case and in view of this, the question of drawing an adverse presumption against the prosecution in this case is not proper and should not arise.
